extracted.intended_audience: readers and students of moral philosophy; philosophers; educated general public
extracted.subtask_description: A 19th-century philosophical essay arguing that compassion (pity) is the primary moral motive and that moral concern extends to animals; includes historical, linguistic, legal, and empirical examples supporting this thesis.

rubrics_metrics.name: Compassion as primary moral motive
rubrics_metrics.description: The original stimulus of true morality is Compassion.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Explained as the root cause of disinterested moral action; illustrated by contrast (e.g., cheating the treasury vs cheating a poor person) showing that blame and self-reproach arise chiefly from the suffering caused to others rather than mere infringement of law.

rubrics_metrics.name: Moral weight tied to victim's suffering
rubrics_metrics.description: Self-accusation and spectators' blame are not furnished directly by the infringement of the law, but chiefly by the suffering thereby brought upon others.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: defrauding the exchequer is less condemnatory than defrauding a poor person; the fraud by a confidential employé is a 'double injustice' because it violates trust and causes acute suffering—hence moral culpability increases with the helplessness and suffering of the victim (widows and orphans as worst-case examples).

rubrics_metrics.name: Compassion underpins justice and loving‑kindness
rubrics_metrics.description: Compassion is the root no less of justice than of loving‑kindness; it is more clearly evidenced in loving‑kindness than in justice.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Friends and relations display genuine loving‑kindness primarily when the recipient suffers. The text uses social examples (friends abandoning the prosperous but aiding the unfortunate) to show that compassion produces protective, comforting, and helpful actions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Compassion as antidote to anger
rubrics_metrics.description: Compassion is the true antidote of anger; picturing another's pain will moderate wrath.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Practical guidance: when inflamed with rage, vividly imagine the other's suffering as if 'This is my work!'—the imaginative identification quenches anger. Supported by poetic citation and argument that viewing the person as 'unfortunate' rapidly ends hostility.

rubrics_metrics.name: Moral duties extend to animals
rubrics_metrics.description: Animals are included under compassion's protecting aegis; beasts have moral claims and are not outside moral consideration.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Critiques the European/Cartesian view that beasts have no rights; points out linguistic and cultural artifices that dehumanize animals. Argues for extending moral sympathy and legal protection to animals, and cites cross-cultural evidence (Indian, Chinese, ancient Greek altars) that compassion for animals has historical support.

rubrics_metrics.name: Continuity between humans and animals (quantitative difference)
rubrics_metrics.description: The truly essential and fundamental part in man and beast is identically the same—the Will; what distinguishes them (intellect) is quantitative, not qualitative.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Argument from zoology and anatomy: cerebral development explains higher human capacities. This continuity is offered as a metaphysical/empirical basis for including animals in moral consideration; counters the claim of an absolute metaphysical gulf.

rubrics_metrics.name: Remorse for cruelty to animals parallels remorse for wrongs to humans
rubrics_metrics.description: People who mistreat animals feel the same kind of remorse and dissatisfaction with themselves as when they wrong fellow humans.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Illustrative anecdotes (hunter remorses after killing monkey/elephant) show that suffering inflicted on animals evokes genuine remorse, implying moral sensitivity toward animals flows from the same source as human-directed conscience.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use law, societies, and public censure to prevent cruelty
rubrics_metrics.description: Legislation and voluntary societies (e.g., Society for the Prevention of Cruelty to Animals) are effective means to lessen animal torture; public exposure/shaming can impose suitable correction when legal penalties are insufficient.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: English legal penalties for cruelty, SPCA's secret watch and interventions, arrests of dog-fight participants, and newspaper naming/shaming as an additional corrective—used as practical guidance for social action to protect animals.

rubrics_metrics.name: Empathy (concrete compassion) is more effective than abstract moral imperatives
rubrics_metrics.description: Nature's method of planting compassion in the heart is more effectual for social well‑being than stern abstract commands of duty; concrete cases awaken compassion where abstract propositions are unintelligible to most people.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Argues that the general populace is 'rude' and engaged in bodily toil, so intuitive, concrete perceptions (compassion sparked by a specific suffering) accomplish moral restraint more readily than theoretical moral laws.

rubrics_metrics.name: Identification amplifies compassion (Rousseau's doctrine)
rubrics_metrics.description: The commiseration will be more energetic the more the spectator identifies with the suffering animal or person.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cites Rousseau: pity arises from transporting oneself into the other's condition—'becoming identified with the living sufferer'—and recommends exposing young people to objects that expand the heart and avoid things that concentrate the egoistic tendency.

rubrics_metrics.name: Limits on vegetarianism and animal labor based on suffering and human need
rubrics_metrics.description: Compassion does not require absolute abstinence from flesh; capacity for pain roughly parallels intelligence, and in northern climates humans need meat to survive; animals may be made to work for humans provided the toil is not excessive.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Argues from a 'natural law' that abstaining from meat in some climates would harm humans more than the animals suffer; recommends easing animal death (e.g., by chloroform) and condemns excessive toil as the boundary where work becomes cruelty.
